blocks.md:
- Work out the length of a dotted half note (dotted minim) and a dotted quarter note (dotted crotchet) by adding half the original note's value.
- Clap or count aloud a short rhythm that uses dotted notes and ties.
- Play a simple melody at the piano that includes dotted notes and a tied note across a bar line.
blocks.label: In this lesson

blocks.md: Quick recap: every note tells you a **pitch** (which key to play) and a **value** (how long to hold it, counted in **beats**). The four values are **whole note** (4 beats), **half note** (2 beats), **quarter note** (1 beat) and **eighth note** (half a beat). Each step down the list halves the length. This lesson adds a **dot**, a small mark that changes a note’s value.

Sometimes you will see a small dot placed just to the right of a note head on the stave. That dot is not decoration. It changes how long the note lasts.

Here is the rule, and it never changes:

**A dot adds half of the note's own value to it.**

In other words: dotted note = original note plus half.

**The dot rule:** dot = original value + half of that value.

You will use this rule every time you see a dotted note.

blocks.text: The dot on a half note

blocks.md:
A **half note** (also called a minim) lasts **2 beats**.

Half of 2 is 1.

So a dotted half note lasts 2 + 1 = **3 beats**.

1. A plain half note lasts 2 beats: count 1, 2.
2. The dot adds half of 2, which is 1 extra beat.
3. Total: 2 + 1 = 3 beats, all held on one note.
blocks.title: Dotted half note: counting it out

blocks.caption: A dotted half note on C. The dot sits just to the right of the note head. Count: 1, 2, 3.

blocks.label: Hear a dotted half note: C held for 3 beats

blocks.md: Dotted half notes appear very often in a piece of music that has a time signature of 3/4, because in these pieces 3 beats fills an entire bar. We will cover time signatures more thoroughly later in this course.

blocks.text: The dot on a quarter note

blocks.md:
A **quarter note** (also called a crotchet) lasts **1 beat**.

Half of 1 is a half-beat (one half-beat is called an **eighth note**, or quaver, and lasts half a beat).

So a dotted quarter note lasts 1 + half = **1 and a half beats**.

1. A plain quarter note lasts 1 beat: count 1.
2. The dot adds half of 1, which is a half-beat.
3. Total: 1 and a half beats.
blocks.title: Dotted quarter note: counting it out

blocks.caption: The first note (C) is a dotted quarter note lasting 1.5 beats. The D that follows is an eighth note (half a beat). Together they fill 2 beats. The E is a plain half note filling the last 2 beats.

blocks.label: Hear the dotted-quarter note rhythm: C (long) then D (short)

blocks.md: The dotted quarter note almost always appears with a short note right after it. That short note is an eighth note (half a beat). Together they add up to 2 beats. You will learn more about this pairing in the next section.
It is easy to rush a dotted note and cut it short. Make sure you hold it for its full value before moving on. Counting out loud really helps.

Sit at your piano. Play middle C (the C roughly in the middle of your keyboard) and hold it while you count aloud: "1, 2, 3". That is a dotted half note. Now play C again and count: "1 and 2" followed by a C on "and". That is a dotted quarter note followed by an eighth note. Repeat each one a few times until the length feels natural in your hands.

blocks.label: Play middle C and hold it: count 1, 2, 3 for the dotted half note, or 1-and for the dotted quarter note

items.prompt: A half note lasts 2 beats. How many beats does a dotted half note last?
items.explain: The dot adds half of the half note's own value. Half of 2 is 1. So 2 + 1 = 3 beats.

items.prompt: A quarter note lasts 1 beat. What does the dot add to a dotted quarter note?
items.explain: The dot always adds half of the note's own value. Half of 1 beat is a half-beat. So a dotted quarter note lasts 1 and a half beats.

items.prompt: The dot rule works differently depending on which note it is placed after.
items.explain: The rule is always the same: the dot adds half of that note's own value, no matter which note it is placed after.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: What Does a Dot Do?

blocks.md: Middle C (also written as C4) is the white key right in the middle of the piano. Find it on the keyboard below before you play.

**Play and hold middle C for 3 beats.**

1. Sit at the piano and find middle C with your right hand, using your thumb (finger 1).
2. Press the key down firmly and count out loud: "1, 2, 3".
3. Keep the key held all the way through all three counts. Do not let go early.
4. Repeat four times until the 3-beat length feels natural.

Now try two dotted half notes one after another: C and then E. Each one lasts 3 beats, so each one fills one whole bar in 3/4 time. This simple pattern is a great way to feel how the 3-beat pulse flows from bar to bar.

blocks.caption: Two bars of 3/4 time. Bar 1: dotted half note on C (3 beats). Bar 2: dotted half note on E (3 beats).

blocks.md: Here is what those two notes sound like played one after another.

blocks.label: C then E, each held for 3 beats
C and E highlighted: the two notes in the pattern

blocks.md:
**Play the two-note dotted half note pattern.**

1. Use your right hand. Place your thumb (finger 1) on middle C and your middle finger (finger 3) on E, the white key two notes to the right of C.
2. Play C and count aloud: "1, 2, 3". Keep the key held down for all three counts.
3. Move smoothly to E and count again: "1, 2, 3". Hold E for all three counts.
4. Repeat the whole pattern (C then E) four times at a slow, steady pace.
5. Try to keep your counting even. Each beat should feel the same length as the last.
**Watch out for this.** The most common mistake is lifting the key too early. If you count out loud it is much easier to hold on for the full 3 beats. Keep counting until you reach the next note.

items.prompt: How many beats does a dotted half note last?
items.explain: A half note lasts 2 beats. The dot adds half of that (1 beat), giving 2 + 1 = 3 beats in total.

items.prompt: A dotted half note fills one complete bar in 3/4 time.
items.explain: In 3/4 time each bar holds exactly 3 beats. A dotted half note lasts 3 beats, so it fits perfectly in one bar on its own.

items.prompt: In the two-note pattern above, what is the second note you play?
items.explain: The pattern uses C (bar 1) and then E (bar 2). E is the white key two notes to the right of middle C.

blocks.title: Check Your Understanding: The Dotted Half note

blocks.text: The Dotted Quarter Note and Its Pair

blocks.md: A dotted quarter note lasts **1.5 beats**, and that leftover half-beat almost always pairs with a short **eighth note** right after it.

**The golden pair:** dotted quarter note (1.5 beats) + eighth note (0.5 beats) = 2 beats total.

You will see this pair constantly in beginner pieces, sight reading and ABRSM Grade 1 repertoire.

blocks.text: Feel it first: a clapping exercise

blocks.md:
Before you read the rhythm on a page, feel it in your hands. This pattern is often described as **long-short, long-short**. The long clap is the dotted quarter note, and the short clap is the eighth note.

Try this now, away from the piano:

1. Say the word **LONG** out loud and clap once, holding that clap for a moment.
2. Say the word **short** and clap once quickly, right after it.
3. Repeat: **LONG short, LONG short, LONG short, LONG short.**
4. Now drop the words and just feel the slight **lilt**, a gentle lean forward on the long, then a quick skip on the short.

That lilt is exactly what the dotted quarter note rhythm sounds like. It gives music a little swing or bounce.

Count aloud as you clap: "1 - and, 2 - and" in 4/4 time. The dotted quarter note lands on the beat number (1), and the eighth note lands on the "and" after beat 2. Counting "and" helps you place that quick note in exactly the right spot.

blocks.text: Now read it on the page

blocks.md: Here is what the dotted quarter note and eighth note pair looks like written on a stave. Notice the dot sitting just to the right of the quarter note head, and the eighth note with its little flag on the stem.

blocks.caption: Two dotted-quarter note + eighth note pairs on middle C, filling a full bar of 4/4. The dot after the first note makes it last 1.5 beats. The flagged eighth note that follows lasts 0.5 beats.

blocks.md: Notice how the bar above contains exactly 4 beats, just as 4/4 requires. Two pairs of dotted quarter note + eighth note, each pair worth 2 beats, gives us 2 + 2 = 4 beats. Everything balances.

blocks.text: Compare: half note vs dotted quarter note + eighth note

blocks.md: A half note is one smooth note lasting 2 beats. A dotted quarter note + eighth note also lasts 2 beats, but it splits them into a long note and a short note. Listen to the difference below.

blocks.label: A half note: one smooth 2-beat note on C
Dotted quarter note + eighth note: long C then quick C (the long-short lilt)

blocks.md: Find middle C on your keyboard. As per usual, it is the white key roughly in the middle, just to the left of a group of two black keys.

blocks.label: Middle C: your starting note for this exercise

blocks.md:
**Long-short at the piano**

1. Sit at the piano and find middle C.
2. Count a steady beat aloud: "1, 2, 3, 4" at a comfortable walking pace.
3. Play C on beat 1 and hold it for 1.5 beats, then play C again quickly on the "and" of beat 2 (the half-beat after 2).
4. Repeat this long-short pair starting on beat 3.
5. Do the whole bar four times in a row until the lilt feels natural.
6. When you are comfortable, try the same pattern using E4 (the white key just above the group of two black keys), then try moving between C and E in the pattern.

The goal is not speed. Go slowly and feel the lean of the long note and the flick of the short one.
Here is a short two-bar melody using dotted quarter note + eighth note pairs. Clap the rhythm first (LONG short, LONG short), then play it slowly on the piano.
blocks.title: A simple melody using the dotted quarter note rhythm

blocks.caption: A two-bar phrase built from dotted quarter note + eighth note pairs. Clap it, then play it on the white keys starting on E4.

blocks.label: Listen to the melody above (long-short lilt): E D C D, E E

items.prompt: A dotted quarter note lasts how many beats?
items.explain: A quarter note lasts 1 beat. The dot adds half of that (half a beat), so 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 beats.

items.prompt: A dotted quarter note is almost always followed by which note value?
items.explain: An eighth note lasts half a beat. Dotted quarter note (1.5 beats) + eighth note (0.5 beats) = 2 beats, making a complete and balanced pair.

items.prompt: A dotted quarter note followed by an eighth note lasts the same total time as one half note.
items.explain: A half note lasts 2 beats. A dotted quarter note (1.5 beats) plus an eighth note (0.5 beats) also adds up to 2 beats. The total duration is the same, but the sound is different: one smooth note versus a long-short lilt.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: The Dotted Quarter note

blocks.md:
A **tie** is a curved line that connects two noteheads on **the same pitch**. That means both notes are the same letter name, sitting in the same position on the stave.

Here is the key rule: you do **not** play the second note again. You press the key once, hold it down, and count both note values together as one continuous sound.

A tie = one press, two values added together.
The second notehead is just a signal to keep holding.

Let's look at a simple example. Below you can see a half note (a note worth 2 beats) tied to a quarter note (a note worth 1 beat). A **half note** is a hollow notehead with a stem. A **quarter note** is a filled notehead with a stem. The curved line between them is the tie.

M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C clef=treble
C2-C z
blocks.caption: A half note C (2 beats) tied to a quarter note C (1 beat). Play C once and hold for 3 beats.

blocks.md: Because 2 beats plus 1 beat equals 3 beats, you hold that single C for a full 3 beats. Count aloud as you hold it: "1 ... 2 ... 3".

blocks.label: C held for 3 beats (half note tied to quarter note)

blocks.md:
Sit at your piano and find Middle C (the C roughly in the middle of the keyboard). Press it down firmly with your right-hand first finger.

1. Count "1, 2" for the half note, keeping the key held down the whole time.
2. On beat 3, do NOT lift and replay. Just keep holding and count "3".
3. Lift your finger after beat 3.

Repeat this four or five times, counting out loud each time. The goal is to feel that single, smooth sound lasting all three beats.

blocks.label: Play Middle C and hold it for 3 beats

blocks.text: Ties vs. Slurs: An Important Contrast

blocks.md:
You will soon come across another curved line that looks almost identical: the **slur**. It is easy to mix these two up, so let's be clear about the difference right away.

A **slur** connects two or more notes that are **different pitches**. It is a performance instruction meaning play those notes smoothly, flowing from one to the next. You **do** play every note under a slur.

A **tie** connects two notes that are **the same pitch**. You play only the first one and hold.

**Tie:** Same pitch, same line on the stave. One press, add the values.

**Slur:** Different pitches, different lines or spaces. Play each note, but smoothly.

blocks.md: When you see a curved line, ask yourself one quick question: are the two noteheads on the **same** pitch or **different** pitches? Same pitch means it is a tie. Different pitches means it is a slur.

In printed music, ties and slurs can look very similar at a glance. Always check the pitch of both noteheads before deciding what to do. Getting this wrong is one of the most common beginner mistakes, so developing the habit of checking early will save you a lot of confusion later.

items.prompt: You see a curved line connecting two noteheads. Both noteheads are on the same pitch. What should you do?
items.explain: A tie means you play only the first note and hold it for the total of both values added together. The second notehead is not played again.
options: Play the first note, then play the second note immediately after.
Play the first note once and hold it for the combined value of both notes.
Skip both notes and move on.
Play both notes at the same time as a chord.

items.prompt: A half note (2 beats) tied to a quarter note (1 beat) gives you a note that lasts 3 beats.
items.explain: Correct. A tie adds the two note values together: 2 beats plus 1 beat equals 3 beats of one continuous held sound.

items.prompt: What is the key difference between a tie and a slur?
items.explain: A tie always joins two notes of the same pitch into one held sound. A slur joins notes of different pitches and tells you to play them smoothly, but you still play each note.
options: A tie is curved and a slur is straight.
A tie connects notes on the same pitch; a slur connects notes on different pitches.
A tie is only used in slow music; a slur is only used in fast music.
There is no difference. They mean the same thing.

blocks.title: Check your understanding: What Is a Tie?

blocks.md:
You already know that a tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound. Now let's look at the most common place you will see a tie in real music: crossing a bar line.

A **bar line** is the vertical line on the stave that divides music into equal units of time called **bars** (sometimes called measures). In 4/4 time, every bar holds exactly four quarter note beats, no more and no less.

**The problem a tie solves.** Sometimes you want a note to ring for, say, six beats. But in 4/4, a bar can only hold four beats. You cannot write a six-beat note inside one bar. The solution: write a note that fills the beats left in the first bar, then tie it to another note at the start of the next bar. Together, they sound as one long, unbroken note.

Here is a common example. Imagine you want a note to start on beat 3 and last for three beats total. Beat 3 and beat 4 sit inside bar 1. But beat 1 of bar 2 belongs to the next bar. You cannot fit all three beats into bar 1. So you write a half note (two beats) on beat 3 of bar 1, then tie it to a quarter note (one beat) at the start of bar 2.

blocks.abc:
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C C G2- | G z2 z
blocks.caption: The G starts on beat 3 of bar 1 as a half note (2 beats), then ties across the bar line to a quarter note G on beat 1 of bar 2. Together they last 3 beats without any break in the sound.

blocks.md: Notice the curved line stretching from the half note G at the end of bar 1 to the quarter note G at the start of bar 2. That curve is the tie. You play the first G and keep holding it. You do **not** play the second G again. It is a continuation, not a new note.

**A quick way to tell a tie from a slur.** A tie always connects two notes of exactly the **same pitch**. A slur connects notes of **different** pitches and means something else entirely. If both noteheads sit on the same line or space, it is a tie.

**Watch out for this mistake.** When you see a tied note at the start of a bar, do not press the key again. Pressing it again would make a second sound and break the tie. Simply keep the key held down from the previous bar.

Using the two-bar phrase below, here is how to count every beat aloud:

- Bar 1, beat 1: play C, say "one"
- Bar 1, beat 2: play C, say "two"
- Bar 1, beat 3: play G (hold it), say "three"
- Bar 1, beat 4: G is still ringing, say "four" (do not replay)
- Bar 2, beat 1: G is still ringing (do not replay), say "one"
- Bar 2, beats 2, 3, 4: rest, say "two, three, four"

The G lasts from beat 3 of bar 1 right through to the end of beat 1 of bar 2. That is three full beats of one unbroken sound.
blocks.title: Counting through the tie

blocks.caption: Your practice phrase. Count every beat aloud as you play. The tied G spans beats 3 and 4 of bar 1, then beat 1 of bar 2.

blocks.label: Hear the phrase: C C, then G held for 3 beats
The notes in this phrase: C4 and G4

blocks.md:
Sit at the piano and find middle C (C4) and the G just above it (G4).

1. Set a slow, steady pulse, about one beat per second.
2. Play and count the phrase exactly as written:
   - Beat 1: play C4
   - Beat 2: play C4
   - Beat 3: play G4 and hold it down
   - Beat 4: keep holding G4, count "four" but do not press again
   - Bar 2, beat 1: keep holding G4, count "one" but do not press again
   - Beats 2, 3, 4 of bar 2: lift your finger and rest
3. Repeat four times. Count out loud every single beat. If the tied G gets a second press by accident, slow down and try again.

**Why this matters in real music.** Ties across bar lines appear constantly in songs and classical pieces. Whenever a melody note needs to feel like it floats over a bar line without stopping, a tie is the tool. Hearing and feeling that long, unbroken sound, even when the bar line arrives, is a key skill you will use in almost every piece you learn.

items.prompt: In 4/4 time, a half note starts on beat 3 of bar 1 and is tied to a quarter note on beat 1 of bar 2. How many beats does the note sound for in total?
items.explain: The half note lasts for beats 3 and 4 of bar 1 (two beats), and the tied quarter note adds one more beat at the start of bar 2. That gives three beats of continuous sound.

items.prompt: When you reach the tied note at the start of bar 2, you should press the key again to show the new bar has begun.
items.explain: A tie means the note continues without any new press. Pressing the key again would create a second attack and break the held sound. You simply keep the key held down.

items.prompt: Why would a composer use a tie across a bar line rather than just writing a longer note value inside one bar?
items.explain: A bar can only hold a fixed number of beats. If the note starts mid-bar and needs to continue into the next bar, a tie is the only way to write that continuous sound across the bar line.
options: To make the music look more complicated
Because the note needs to last longer than the remaining beats in the bar allow
Because ties are louder than single notes
To tell the performer to play the note twice

blocks.text: Putting It All Together at the Piano

blocks.md:
You have learned what dotted notes do, and you have learned what a tie does. Now it is time to use them both in a real piece of music.

Below is a short 8-bar melody in C major. C major simply means it uses the white notes of the piano, starting and centring on C. The melody sits in the treble clef (the curly symbol at the start of the stave, used for the higher-pitched notes you play with your right hand).

Take a moment to look through the music before you play a single note. That is the habit we are building right now.
**Before you play each bar, check:** Is there a dot after any note? Is there a tie joining a note to the next bar? Spotting these first stops surprises mid-phrase.

blocks.caption: 8-bar melody in C major using dotted quarter note + eighth note pairs (bars 2 and 4) and a tie across the bar line (bars 5 to 6).

blocks.md: Let us walk through the key moments bar by bar.

blocks.text: Bar by Bar: What to Watch For

blocks.md:
A quarter note (one beat) with a dot becomes one and a half beats. The short eighth note (half a beat) that follows fills the gap to make two beats total. Together they feel like a gentle long-SHORT lilt.

Count aloud: "1 - and - 2 - and" where the dot note lands on 1, and the eighth note lands on the "and" of beat 2.

In bar 2 that means: G dotted (beats 1 and the "and" and beat 2) then F short (the "and" of beat 2), then E held for beats 3 and 4.
blocks.title: Bars 2 and 4: The dotted quarter note and eighth note

blocks.label: Dotted quarter note and eighth note: G then F (as in bar 2)

blocks.md:
Remember, a tie is a curved line joining two notes of the same pitch. You play the first note and keep holding it. You do NOT play the second note again.

In bar 5, after the opening G you play C and hold it. The tie carries that C across the bar line into bar 6, so the C rings out for 4 beats in total before the melody moves on to B and A.
blocks.title: Bars 5 to 6: The tie across the bar line

blocks.caption: The tie: C is held from bar 5 into bar 6. Do not re-strike the tied C at the start of bar 6.

blocks.label: Bars 5-6: G, then C held across the bar line, then B and A
The notes used in this melody (C to D above middle C)

blocks.md:
Set a slow, comfortable pulse. A metronome around 60 beats per minute works well, but tapping your foot is just as good.

Count every beat aloud: "1, 2, 3, 4" for every bar. Say the number out loud even when you are holding a note. This keeps you anchored in time and helps you feel exactly when the held note ends.

Play through the 8-bar melody once at a slow tempo. Count aloud on every beat. When you reach bar 2 or bar 4, say "long... short" to yourself for the dotted quarter note and eighth note. When you reach bar 5, say "hold... hold" as C rings across the bar line. It is completely fine if you need to stop and restart. Slow and accurate beats fast and messy every time.

Once you have made it through slowly with the counting, try a second play-through. Keep the same tempo, but this time let yourself listen to the melody rather than focusing on the counting.

Notice how the dotted rhythm in bars 2 and 4 gives the melody a little bounce. Notice how the tied C in bars 5 and 6 creates a moment of calm before the melody moves on. Those effects are exactly what the composer controls with dots and ties.

blocks.label: Listen to the full melody from start to finish

blocks.md: **The pre-bar check habit:** Before you play any new bar, glance ahead at the next one. Look for a dot (it adds half the note's value) or a tie (it means hold, do not re-strike). This single habit will save you from the most common rhythm mistakes.

Play the melody a third time, now at a tempo that feels natural and comfortable to you. After you finish, ask yourself two questions: Where did I feel most confident? Where did I need to slow down? Make a note of the bar numbers so you can target those spots in your next practice session.

items.prompt: In bars 5 and 6 of the melody, C is tied across the bar line. What should you do when you reach the C at the start of bar 6?
items.explain: A tie means you hold the first note for the combined length of both notes. You never re-strike the tied note. The C you played in bar 5 simply keeps ringing into bar 6.
options: Play C again with a fresh finger press
Keep holding the C from bar 5 and do not re-strike it
Rest for two beats, then play C
Play C more softly than in bar 5

items.prompt: In bars 2 and 4 the dotted quarter note and eighth note pattern gives the melody a long-SHORT feel. How many beats does the dotted quarter note last?
items.explain: A quarter note lasts 1 beat. A dot adds half of that, so half a beat more. 1 plus half equals 1 and a half beats. The eighth note then fills the remaining half beat.

items.prompt: A good practice habit is to look ahead at the next bar before you play it, checking for any dots or ties.
items.explain: Spotting a dot or a tie before you arrive at it gives you time to prepare the right finger action. It is one of the most useful habits you can build at this stage.

blocks.md: Dotted notes and ties are everywhere in real music. The gentle lilt of a waltz comes almost entirely from the dotted half note, which fills three beats and gives the music room to breathe. The dotted quarter note appears in countless melodies, from folk songs to hymns, wherever a rhythm needs a little skip or swing. Ties let composers hold a note across a bar line, creating a smooth, flowing sound that feels longer than any single note value can provide on its own. Next time you sit at the piano and open a piece, look for the dot beside a note head or the curved line joining two identical notes. You will find them in almost every line of music you ever play.

- **note value**: how long a note lasts, measured in beats
- **whole note**: a note that lasts four beats (also called a semibreve)
- **half note**: a note that lasts two beats (also called a minim)
- **quarter note**: a note that lasts one beat (also called a crotchet)
- **eighth note**: a note that lasts half a beat (also called a quaver)
- **dot**: a small dot placed after a note head that adds half the note's own value to its length
- **dotted half note**: a half note with a dot, lasting three beats (two plus one)
- **dotted quarter note**: a quarter note with a dot, lasting one and a half beats (one plus a half)
- **tie**: a curved line joining two notes of the same pitch, meaning you play the first note and hold it for the combined length of both, without replaying the second
- **slur**: a curved line over two or more notes of different pitches, meaning play them smoothly and connectedly in one phrase (unlike a tie, which joins notes of the same pitch)
- **bar line**: a vertical line on the stave that divides music into equal groups of beats called bars

- Every note has a value that tells you how many beats to hold it.
- A dot after a note adds half of that note's value to its length.
- A dotted half note lasts three beats: two beats plus one.
- A dotted quarter note lasts one and a half beats: one beat plus a half.
- A tie is a curved line between two notes of the same pitch. You play once and hold for the total length of both notes combined.
- Ties can cross a bar line, letting a single held note stretch further than one bar allows.
- When reading music, always check for dots and ties before you start playing so the rhythm makes sense straight away.

items.prompt: A plain half note (half note) lasts for 2 beats. How many beats does a dotted half note last?
items.explain: A dot adds half of the note's own value. Half of 2 beats is 1 beat, so 2 + 1 = 3 beats. A dotted half note lasts for 3 beats.

items.prompt: A dotted quarter note (dotted quarter note) is worth 1.5 beats. Which pair of notes adds up to exactly the same length?
items.explain: A quarter note lasts 1 beat and an eighth note lasts half a beat. Together they make 1.5 beats, which is the same as a dotted quarter note.
options: A quarter note (1 beat) tied to another quarter note (1 beat)
A quarter note (1 beat) tied to an eighth note (half a beat)
A half note (2 beats) tied to an eighth note (half a beat)
Two eighth notes (half a beat each)

items.prompt: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch, and you play them as one long sound without lifting your finger between them.
items.explain: A tie is a curved line connecting two notes on the same pitch. You press the key once and hold it for the combined length of both notes. You do not replay the second note.

items.prompt: A quarter note (quarter note) lasts 1 beat. If you add a dot to it, how many beats does the dotted quarter note last? Write your answer as a number or fraction (for example: 1.5 or 1 and a half).
items.explain: The dot adds half the quarter note's value. Half of 1 beat is half a beat, so 1 + 0.5 = 1.5 beats.

items.prompt: Look at a bar in 4/4 time (4 beats per bar). The bar contains a half note (2 beats) and there is a tie that carries into the next bar. What does that tie tell you to do?
items.explain: A tie across a bar line means you hold the key down continuously from the note in the first bar right into the next bar. You do not strike the key again at the bar line.
options: Play the tied note again at the start of the next bar
Rest for those beats at the start of the next bar
Hold the note over from the first bar into the next bar without replaying it
Play the note louder where the tie begins
